displayQuote: A constitution should be short and obscure

meta.title: Who really said "A constitution should be short and obscure"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Napoleon never said it. The line is a paraphrase of Talleyrand’s 1802 quip to Roederer over the Cisalpine constitution. The documented source, traced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A constitution should be short and obscure'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Napoleon — it was Talleyrand’s sardonic aside to Roederer in 1802, recorded in Roederer’s memoirs. Here’s the real story.

answer.label: Not Napoleon — a quip by Talleyrand
answer.sourceLine: Napoleon never proclaimed this as a maxim. The line comes from an 1802 exchange over a draft constitution for the Cisalpine (Italian) Republic: Napoleon’s councillor Pierre-Louis Roederer favored a very short text and was calling it ‘short and…’ when Talleyrand cut in, ‘Yes: short and obscure.’ The crisp one-liner pinned on Napoleon is a later paraphrase of that witticism, recorded in Roederer’s memoirs.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Draft constitution for the Cisalpine Republic, 1802

source.excerpt: Roederer had drawn up two plans of a constitution for the Cisalpine — one very short, leaving much to the discretion of the President, the other precise and detailed — and told Talleyrand to advise Bonaparte to adopt the former, as it was ‘short and—’ ‘Yes,’ interrupted Talleyrand, ‘short and obscure.’
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under ‘Misattributed’, attributing the words to Talleyrand’s interruption of Roederer, not to Napoleon.
Napoleon historian Shannon Selin names it among ‘10 Things Napoleon Never Said’, dating the exchange to an 1802 constitution for the Cisalpine Republic in Italy.
Both trace the anecdote to Roederer’s own Œuvres (vol. III, p. 428), as relayed in John Holland Rose’s The Life of Napoleon I (1902).
source.excerptNote: Paraphrased from Roederer’s memoirs as recounted by John Holland Rose; the popular ‘A constitution should be short and obscure’ compresses this anecdote into a maxim and reassigns it to Napoleon.
source.rightsNote: The documented exchange is preserved in Roederer’s Œuvres (1854) and John Holland Rose’s The Life of Napoleon I (1902), both long in the public domain in the United States. The polished maxim credited to Napoleon is a later, anonymous paraphrase with no author of record.

author.name: Charles Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord
author.heading: Whose words these really are
author.metaLine: 1754–1838 · French diplomat & foreign minister under Napoleon
author.bio: Talleyrand was the supreme survivor of French politics, serving the monarchy, the Revolution, Napoleon, and the restored Bourbons in turn. A famed wit and cynic, he was Napoleon’s foreign minister when Roederer sought his counsel on the Cisalpine constitution — and his sardonic interjection, not any pronouncement by Napoleon, is the true origin of the ‘short and obscure’ line.

misattribution.heading: How Napoleon got the credit
misattribution.intro: The sentence reads like a cynical maxim of statecraft, so it drifted naturally toward the era’s most quotable strongman — even though the words were spoken about a constitution Napoleon was reviewing, not by him.

items.why: Quote sites from BrainyQuote to AZQuotes print it as a bare Napoleon aphorism with no source; it appears in none of his writings or recorded remarks.
The phrase ‘short and obscure’ was Talleyrand’s sardonic completion of Roederer’s sentence, as Wikiquote documents from Roederer’s memoirs.

misattribution.truthLine: A witticism Talleyrand tossed off in 1802 — recorded by Roederer, not proclaimed by Napoleon — hardened over time into a fake Napoleon maxim.

context.heading: Why the phrase stuck
lead: The remark captures a real strategy of the Consulate era: constitutions drafted to concentrate power by leaving key questions vague. The Constitution of the Year VIII that installed Napoleon as First Consul was famously terse and had no declaration of rights — which is why later historians could describe it as ‘short and obscure’ and why the quip found a home near Napoleon’s name.

But the specific exchange concerned a constitution for the Cisalpine (soon the Italian) Republic in 1802, and the sting belonged to Talleyrand — a courtier famous precisely for such double-edged asides.
detailsBody: Roederer and Talleyrand were both advising Napoleon, then Consul, on reorganizing the sister republics of northern Italy. Roederer’s preference for a brief text that left wide latitude to the executive was exactly the sort of design the quip skewered — short on paper, elastic in practice.
